types-values.summary: Know the primitive types, how equality and truthiness work, and the handful of quirks every interviewer asks about.
points: There are seven primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, null); everything else is an object, including arrays and functions.
`===` compares without type conversion; `==` converts first. Use `===` by default, except `x == null` as shorthand for null-or-undefined.
The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Every object is truthy, even `[]` and `{}`.
`typeof null` is `"object"` (a historical bug) and `NaN !== NaN`. Test with `value === null` and `Number.isNaN(value)`.
Numbers are IEEE 754 doubles, so `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`. Compare with a tolerance, or work in integers (such as cents).
traps: The global `isNaN('abc')` is true because it coerces; `Number.isNaN('abc')` is false.
`Object.is(0, -0)` is false even though `0 === -0` is true.

objects-arrays.summary: Objects and arrays are references. Know which methods mutate, which return new values, and how to copy safely.
points: Assigning an object or array copies the reference, not the value. Two variables can point at the same array.
`const` stops you reassigning a variable; it does not make the object immutable.
Non-mutating methods (`map`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat`, `toSorted`) return new arrays; mutating ones (`push`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`) change the original.
Spread and `Object.assign` make shallow copies. Use `structuredClone` for deep copies that keep Dates, Maps and Sets.
`Object.freeze` is shallow; nested objects stay mutable.
traps: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` turns Dates into strings and drops `undefined` and functions.
`sort()` sorts as strings by default: `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`.

closures-scope.summary: Functions remember the scope they were created in. Understand block scope, hoisting and the classic loop bug.
points: A closure is a function plus the variables it can reach from where it was defined, even after the outer function returns.
`var` is function-scoped and hoisted as `undefined`; `let` and `const` are block-scoped and sit in a temporal dead zone until declared.
Closures in a `var` loop share one variable; `let` gives each iteration its own binding.
Factories (functions returning functions) use closures to keep private state, like a counter.
traps: Reading a `let` variable before its declaration throws a ReferenceError; reading a `var` gives `undefined`.

this-binding.summary: `this` is decided by how a function is called, except in arrow functions, which inherit it.
points: Method call `obj.fn()` sets `this` to `obj`. A plain call `fn()` sets it to `undefined` in strict mode (modules and classes are always strict).
`call` and `apply` invoke immediately with a chosen `this`; `bind` returns a new function with `this` fixed.
Arrow functions have no `this` of their own; they use the surrounding scope's, so they suit callbacks inside methods.
`new Fn()` creates a fresh object and binds `this` to it.
traps: Passing `obj.method` as a callback (to `setTimeout` or an event listener) loses `this` unless you bind it or wrap it in an arrow function.

promises.summary: Promises represent future values. Know the combinators and how to run work in parallel.
points: An `async` function always returns a promise; `await` unwraps it or throws on rejection, so `try/catch` works.
`Promise.all` fails fast; `allSettled` reports every outcome; `race` takes the first to settle; `any` takes the first success.
Work runs in parallel when every promise is created before you wait on it. `await` inside a loop runs the steps one by one.
Unhandled rejections are reported by the runtime. Always return or await the promises you create.
traps: `forEach` does not wait for async callbacks; use `for...of` with `await`, or `Promise.all(array.map(...))`.

event-loop.summary: One main thread runs tasks one at a time; microtasks run between them. That explains most ordering puzzles.
points: The current script (a task) always runs to completion before anything else.
After each task, the microtask queue (promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`) is drained completely.
Then the next task runs: a timer, an event, a message. Rendering happens between tasks.
Long synchronous work blocks input and rendering; split it up or move it to a Web Worker.
traps: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` does not run immediately. It waits for the current task and all microtasks.

dom-events.summary: Select elements, listen for events, and use bubbling to handle many elements with one listener.
points: `querySelector` and `querySelectorAll` accept any CSS selector.
Events bubble from the target up through its ancestors, which enables event delegation with `event.target.closest(...)`.
`preventDefault()` cancels the browser's default action; `stopPropagation()` stops bubbling. They are independent.
`DOMContentLoaded` fires when the DOM is ready; `load` waits for images and other resources too.
traps: The `input` event fires on every keystroke; `change` fires when the value is committed.

web-apis.summary: The browser APIs you use every day: fetch, storage, cancellation and visibility.
points: `fetch` rejects only on network errors. Check `response.ok` for HTTP errors.
Cancel requests with an `AbortController` signal; build deadlines with `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`.
`localStorage` persists and `sessionStorage` lasts one tab session; both store strings only.
`IntersectionObserver` tells you when elements become visible, which suits lazy loading and infinite scroll.
traps: Storage can throw (private mode, quota), so wrap access in try/catch.
